notes.b: Rural settlement is the farmhouses, hamlets (very small groups of houses) and villages in the countryside. Its pattern is the way the buildings are spread over the land, and geographers sort patterns into three types.
points: Dispersed: individual farmhouses scattered across the land, each on its own farm.
Clustered (also called nucleated): buildings grouped together in one place, usually for a shared reason such as a crossroads or a water supply.
Linear (also called ribbon): houses strung along a line such as a road, a coast road, a valley or a ridge.
Clustered and nucleated mean the same pattern, and linear is the same as ribbon when it extends out of a town along approach roads, so there are three patterns, not four.
In Census 2016 (the national count of the population), about 63% of Ireland's population lived in urban areas and about 37% in rural areas.
notes.tip: Clustered and nucleated are one pattern, and linear is the same as ribbon when it extends out of a town along approach roads. Don't present them as four separate patterns.

notes.b: Dispersed settlement is the dominant rural pattern in Ireland. It exists for farming, historical and physical reasons.
points: Irish farms are family-owned, and each family lives on its own holding (its own farm), so the houses end up spread out across the countryside.

The Land Commission was set up in 1881 under the Land Law (Ireland) Act 1881. After the Land Acts, consolidation of holdings (joining scattered plots into one compact farm) moved houses out of clusters onto individual farms.
The Wyndham Land Act of 1903 helped tenants to buy their holdings, which strengthened the pattern of families owning and living on their own land.
Fertile, well-drained lowland with plentiful water lets houses be built almost anywhere, because no site is much better than another.
Pastoral farming (rearing animals, especially cattle and sheep) keeps the farmer close to the animals, so the house sits on the farm.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the reasons for settlement patterns in Ireland. Give a historical reason (the Land Acts and consolidation) as well as farming and physical ones.

notes.b: Buildings are grouped together where a shared reason made the site worth using. Each reason below explains why people chose to build close together instead of apart.
points: Route focus: a crossroads where roads meet brings travellers and trade, so buildings gather there.
A bridging point or ford (a shallow place where a river can be crossed) draws settlement because routes must pass through it.
A church, a castle or estate gates act as a focus, and people settle beside them for work, worship or protection.
Defence: a hill or other defensible site was chosen so the settlement could be defended.
Water supply at a spring or well gives a wet-point site, where people settle because they need water.
A dry-point site is a patch of dry ground above flood land, chosen so houses stay dry.
A harbour is the reason for a fishing village, because the boats and the catch are landed there.
Services such as a shop, pub, school and Garda station (police station) gather in the cluster, which then attracts further settlement.
Estate village: Enniskerry, Co. Wicklow, lies at the gates of the Powerscourt estate (a large landowner's property), and Adare, Co. Limerick, grew by the Dunraven estate, with thatched cottages.
notes.tip: Link each cluster to a named cause (crossroads, bridge, wet-point, dry-point, harbour and so on) and use the word nucleated for it.

notes.b: Before the Famine many farmers in the west lived in clachans instead of on separate farms. The way land was held in common explains why.
points: A clachan is a cluster of farmhouses of related families, with no church, shop or other services. It is not a village, because a village has services.

Rundale was a landholding system in which families worked land in common, in scattered strips of infield (the better land near the houses) and outfield (poorer land further out). It explains the clachan; it is not a settlement pattern.
Clachans and rundale were common in the west before the Famine.
The Great Famine (1845-49), when the potato crop failed and many people died or emigrated, hit the clachan districts of the west hardest.

Clachans broke up as the population fell and holdings were consolidated. The Congested Districts Board, set up in 1891 for the poor western districts, consolidated holdings, built roads and piers, and rehoused families on separate farms.
The Land Commission also moved houses onto individual farms, which is how dispersed settlement replaced the clachans.
A few clachans survive in the west.
notes.tip: A clachan has no church, shop or other services, so don't call it a village. Rundale is a landholding system, not a settlement pattern: mention it only to explain clachans.

notes.b: Linear settlement is the third pattern. Houses line up along a feature that offers a route or dry, firm ground.
points: Houses are strung along a line: a road, a coast road, a valley floor, a river or a raised ridge such as an esker (a long ridge of gravel left by a glacier) or the edge of a drumlin (an oval hill of glacial deposit).
Linear settlement avoids marshy or steep land, because it is hard and costly to build on.
notes.tip: Linear is the same as ribbon when it extends out of a town along approach roads.

notes.b: Some land on a map has no settlement at all, and exams ask you to explain why. There is more on reading this from OS maps in Map interpretation.
points: Uplands are steep, exposed and have poor soils, so they are hard to build on and farm.
Bogs are wet, poorly drained land, so houses cannot be built safely on them.
Flood plains (flat land beside a river that floods) are unsuitable for houses because of the risk of flooding.
Lakes take up land that could hold houses.
Forestry plantations are large areas of planted trees with no houses.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain both the absence of settlement and the high density of settlement in parts of a map. Give one reason for each type of empty land.

notes.b: Two European examples show how planning and history shape rural settlement very differently from the Irish pattern.
points: Noordoostpolder, Netherlands, a polder (land drained from water) drained in 1942, is a planned rural landscape with a central town, Emmeloord, ringed by ten planned villages. There is more on this in Urban settlement: site, hierarchy, hinterland and central place theory.

In southern Italy, the Mezzogiorno's rural population lived in hilltop villages. The 1950 land reform scattered new farmhouses on reclaimed lowlands, so settlement moved from clustered to dispersed. There is more on this in A Peripheral European Region: the Mezzogiorno.

notes.b: Ribbon development is houses built one plot deep along the roads leading out of towns and villages, and along rural roads generally. Several pressures made roadsides the favoured building sites.
points: Sites are cheaper than in towns, so buyers get more for their money.
Road frontage gives access to services such as electricity, water mains and phone or broadband lines, which already run along the road.
Farmers sold roadside sites, because these were the easiest plots to sell.
People wanted rural living near a town, with the countryside around them and work or schools close by.
Car ownership made commuting (travelling daily to work) and rural living practical.
Planning control was historically weak, so few limits stopped houses going up along roads.
Tax incentives and the property boom of the Celtic Tiger (the period of rapid economic growth in Ireland) encouraged building.
notes.tip: A short question asks you to define ribbon development: houses one plot deep along roads. Longer questions ask for its causes and problems.

notes.b: Ribbon housing suits the people who live in it, but it causes problems for roads, services, the environment and towns.
points: Traffic hazards: many entrances onto fast roads, because every house needs its own access and drivers have to slow or turn.
It is costly to service. School buses, post, waste collection, water and sewers must all reach scattered houses, which are far apart.
Septic tanks (private tanks that treat a house's own sewage) can pollute groundwater and private wells.
Loss of scenic landscape, because the roadsides fill with houses.
Car dependence: residents need a car for almost every journey, as shops and services are far away.
Town centres decline as people live outside them and spend less in them.
The boundary between town and country becomes blurred, because houses line the roads where the town should end.
notes.tip: A short question may ask for one problem of one-off housing. Give the problem and its reason, such as the cost of servicing scattered houses.

notes.b: Rural people often see ribbon housing differently, because it helps keep their communities going.
points: Ribbon development keeps rural populations, schools, GAA clubs and shops alive, because they need people living nearby to survive.
It lets families live near relatives and farms.
Housing is cheaper than in towns.

notes.b: Planning is how the State controls where building takes place. It works through the local authority (the county or city council), with plans made at county and local level.
points: Planning permission is granted by the local authority.
Decisions can be appealed to An Bord Pleanála, the national planning appeals board, set up in 1977. It was renamed An Coimisiún Pleanála in 2025.
The Planning and Development Act 2000 requires each planning authority to make a County Development Plan every six years.
The County Development Plan sets zoning (deciding which land may be used for housing, industry or farming), rural housing policy, design rules and protected areas.
Local Area Plans cover towns and villages.
notes.tip: Higher Level 30-mark questions can ask about planning strategies in rural areas and their effectiveness, so know the plan, the appeals board and the policies that follow.

notes.b: National policy sets the aims that county plans must follow. Rural housing is treated differently depending on how much pressure an area is under.
points: The National Spatial Strategy (2002) and the National Planning Framework (2018, also called Project Ireland 2040) set rural housing aims. There is more on both in Urban planning and renewal.
Sustainable Rural Housing Guidelines for Planning Authorities, 2005, tell councils how to treat different types of rural area.
In areas under strong urban influence (close to a city or large town), rural houses are limited to people with a local economic or social need, to prevent commuter housing spreading.
In structurally weak areas (areas losing people and jobs), rural housing is encouraged to keep the population.

notes.b: County Development Plans turn national aims into rules for each county. These are the typical rural policies.
points: Local-needs criteria restrict who may build a house in some rural areas, for example to those with a local economic or social need.
New entrances onto national and regional roads are restricted, because many entrances onto fast roads are a traffic hazard.
New housing is directed into villages and serviced sites (sites with water and sewers), which avoids scattered one-off houses.
Design guidelines cover siting, materials and hedgerows.
Minimum site sizes apply to septic tanks, so that there is enough land to treat the waste safely.
Scenic areas and views are protected from development.
Land is zoned around towns, so that building is guided to where it is planned.

notes.b: Septic tanks serve houses with no connection to a public sewer, so poorly maintained ones can pollute the water that rural households drink.
points: Water Services (Amendment) Act 2012: domestic septic tanks must be registered, and they are inspected under an EPA (Environmental Protection Agency) plan.
Ireland has about half a million domestic wastewater treatment systems, mostly septic tanks (EPA estimate).
notes.tip: Don't give any septic tank, one-off house or planning refusal figure other than the EPA estimate of about half a million.

notes.b: These programmes respond to rural depopulation (people leaving rural areas) and the decline of services such as post offices, Garda stations and pubs. They aim to sustain rural communities.
points: LEADER, an EU rural development programme, from 1991.
CLÁR, a State programme for rural areas suffering depopulation, from 2001.
The Town and Village Renewal Scheme, from 2016.
Our Rural Future, the Government's rural development policy for 2021-2025, published in 2021, supports remote working hubs (shared workplaces where people can work remotely from home areas).

notes.b: To judge how well rural planning works, weigh the aims against each other and against what has happened.
points: The central tension is keeping rural communities alive while preventing sprawl (unplanned spread of housing).

Local-needs conditions have been criticised as unfair. In 2013 the EU Court of Justice ruled against a Flemish (Belgian) rule restricting who could buy land in some communes, which raised doubts about Irish local-needs conditions.
Planning has reduced ribbon development but has not stopped it.
Villages need sewage treatment before they can take more housing, which limits the policy of directing housing into villages.
notes.tip: Don't say local-needs rules were abolished or illegal: only the 2013 EU ruling on the Flemish rule is established. For effectiveness, say planning has reduced but not stopped ribbon development.

keyTerms.definition: Individual farmhouses scattered across the land, each on its own farm.
Buildings grouped together in one place, also called nucleated settlement.
Houses strung along a line such as a road, valley or ridge.
A cluster of farmhouses of related families, with no church, shop or other services.
A landholding system in which families worked land in common, in scattered strips of infield and outfield.
Houses built one plot deep along roads leading out of towns and villages, and along rural roads.

A domestic wastewater treatment system that must be registered and inspected under an EPA plan.
A plot with services such as water, sewers and electricity provided, where new housing is directed.

questions.prompt: Examine the planning strategies used to manage rural settlement in Ireland.
questions.model: Planning permission is granted by the local authority, with appeals to An Bord Pleanála, set up in 1977 and renamed An Coimisiún Pleanála in 2025. Under the Planning and Development Act 2000, the County Development Plan, made every six years, sets zoning, rural housing policy, design rules and protected areas, and Local Area Plans cover towns and villages. Nationally, the National Spatial Strategy (2002) and the National Planning Framework (2018) set rural housing aims. The Sustainable Rural Housing Guidelines (2005) limit rural housing in areas under strong urban influence to people with a local need, and encourage it in structurally weak areas to keep the population. County plans restrict new entrances onto national and regional roads, direct housing into villages and serviced sites, set design guidelines, set minimum site sizes for septic tanks and protect scenic areas. The Water Services (Amendment) Act 2012 requires septic tanks to be registered and inspected under an EPA plan. Rural development programmes, LEADER (from 1991), CLÁR (from 2001), the Town and Village Renewal Scheme (from 2016) and Our Rural Future (2021–2025), address depopulation and the decline of services. Evaluation: planning has reduced ribbon development but has not stopped it. Local-needs conditions are criticised as unfair, and the 2013 EU Court of Justice ruling on a Flemish rule raised doubts about them. Villages need sewage treatment before they can take more housing, and the tension between keeping rural communities alive and preventing sprawl remains.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain the dispersed and clustered patterns of rural settlement in Ireland.
questions.model: Dispersed settlement: individual farmhouses are scattered, each on its own farm, and it is the dominant Irish pattern. Irish farms are family-owned and each family lives on its holding. Consolidation of holdings after the Land Acts moved houses out of clusters onto individual farms, through the Land Commission (set up in 1881) and the Congested Districts Board (set up in 1891). The Wyndham Land Act of 1903 helped tenants to buy their holdings. Fertile, well-drained lowland with plentiful water allows houses anywhere, and pastoral farming keeps the farmer close to the animals. Clustered settlement: buildings are grouped where a shared reason made the site worth using, such as a crossroads, a bridging point, a church, a castle or estate gates, defence, a spring or well, a dry-point site above flood land, or a harbour. Services such as a shop, pub, school and Garda station gather there. Clachans, clusters of farmhouses of related families with no church or shop, were common in the west before the Famine, when rundale worked land in common in scattered strips. They broke up as holdings were consolidated and houses moved onto individual farms.

questions.prompt: What is ribbon development? Explain two problems it causes.
questions.model: Ribbon development is houses built one plot deep along roads leading out of towns and villages, and along rural roads generally. It was encouraged by cheaper sites than in towns, road frontage with access to services, and car ownership. Problem 1, traffic hazards: many entrances open onto fast roads, so cars enter and leave at many points, creating danger for road users. Problem 2, cost of services: school buses, post, waste collection, water and sewers must all reach scattered houses, which is expensive. Septic tanks can also pollute groundwater and private wells.
